description.narrative: Insatsens mål på lägre sikt är att bidra till att säkerställa tillgång till överkomlig, tillförlitlig, hållbar och modern energi, särskilt förnybar energi, och därigenom ökad tillgång till el för fattiga grupper. Genom anpassad policy och regelverk ämnar programmet stärka förutsättningar för ökade investeringar i förnybar energi, som i förlängningen tillgängliggör förnybara energitjänster. Mål på medellång sikt inom insatsens direkta påverkan är att strategiskt utvalda organisationer ökar sin kapacitet att stärka förutsättningar för investeringar i hållbara energisystem. Rättighetsperspektiv som utgår från behov och efterfrågan hos människor som lever i fattigdom ska genomsyra programmet. Efter genomförd kapacitetsutveckling ska varje deltagande organisation fått: - Ökad kunskap om förnybara energikällor/-teknik och verktyg för att analysera och prioritera de mest lämpliga lösningarna beroende på kontext. - Ökad kunskap om tillgång och efterfrågan på förnybara energisystem och vad som behövs för planering, finansiering och utveckling av sådana. Möjlig klimatfinansiering ingår här. - Förbättrad kunskap om hur institutionella strukturer kan bidra till att främja ett gynnsamt klimat för investeringar i en förnybar energiutbyggnad, vilket möjliggör investeringar i olika typer av energiinfrastruktur. - Förbättrad kunskap om lagstiftning, reglering, prissättning, skatteinstrument, offentlig upphandling av förnybara energisystem. - Utbyte av erfarenheter, metoder och verktyg samt förstärkt ledarskapsförmåga, att genomföra organisatoriskt och institutionellt förändringsarbete, inklusive egna förändringsprocesser och förmåga att sprida och dela med sig av kunskaper och erfarenheter som uppnåtts genom programmet. - Tillgång till ökade internationella och nationella professionella nätverk till stöd för ett effektivt arbete med hållbara investeringar och teknologier för förnybar energi.

International Capacity Development Program aimed at strengthening capacity at strategically selected institutions to develop policies, regulatory frameworks and other conditions for investments in renewable energy technologies and sustainable energy systems by providing energy infrastructure, taking into account the rights perspective, needs and demand of people living in poverty.

Internationellt kapacitetsutvecklingsprogram som syftar till att stärka kapaciteten hos strategiskt utvalda institutioner att utveckla policy, regelverk och andra förutsättningar för investeringar i förnybar energiteknik och hållbara energisystem genom att tillhandahålla energiinfrastruktur med beaktande av rättighetsperspektiv, behov och efterfrågan hos människor som lever i fattigdom.

sector.narrative: Energy generation, renewable sources - multiple technologies

description.narrative:
The overall purpose of the Renewable Energy ITP programme was to contribute to strengthening the conditions for investments in renewable energy to provide modern and sustainable energy systems, including all forms of renewable energy such as solar, wind, hydro, bio, and geothermal energy in participated countries. The intermediate goal for the intervention was: Participating strategic organisations in participating countries have increased level of capacity to lead change processes towards changed legal frameworks and strengthened incentives for investments in sustainable energy systems with consideration of rights, needs, and demands of people living in poverty which ultimately shall lead to that sustainable energy systems exist in the targeted countries.
Through the programme, 4 cohorts (REP 1 4) implemented between 2018 2023, good results have achieved by the 23 teams from 8 countries participated in the REP and what changes they have made from their change projects to the renewable energy sector in their countries, in terms of knowledge and skills developed, senior organizational leaders engaged, policy development networked and collaboration with other stakeholders in renewable energy development. In total, 105 participants (41% women) from 39 public agencies, NGOs, national development banks and state-owned companies have completed the programme and change projects. For each REP cycle, great emphasis was put on obtaining qualified participants from strategic organisations in the energy sector in each of the participating countries, which were Ethiopia, Kenya, Mozambique, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
During the entire implementation of the intervention, an external evaluator followed the work. To be able to evaluate the results, four different evaluation criteria were used. These were: a) The programmes relevance for participants and the target organisation, b) how the programme was implemented, c) fulfilment of the objectives in relation to the Theory of Change and, d) sustained change of the programme, i.e. how the intervention could be expected to have an impact over a longer period of time. The REPs external review and evaluation has shown the results and impacts the programme has contributed to individual growth, influences made on participated organisations and countries policy in renewable energy, with changes sustained and high impacts made, so positive that the REP will continue to develop further beyond Sidas financing commitments. ITP 2.0 will be run on its own resources and capacity, thanks to the ITP developed and supported by Sida in this phase.
Accumulated results achieved by the REP at country level in relations to the objectives can be summarized as follows: 1. Ethiopia Ethiopia was one of the six countries chosen by Sida as a target country for the first call of the intervention. The intervention involved a total of 9 participants from Ethiopia who participated in three out of the four programmes (REP 1-3). In total 15 persons were accepted to the programme, but 6 persons dropped out in different stages. This means that 40% of the admitted participants did not complete the programme, which is the highest level among the 8 participating countries. The Country Teams from Ethiopia implemented three Change Projects addressing different problems in the energy sector in Ethiopia, which contributed to building capacity to develop the energy sector among several people who work at relevant and strategic organisations, as well as to promoting a sustainable energy system in the country. • REP 1 Ethiopia: Long-Term Renewable Energy Sources Development Plan with Modelling Tool, where developing the ability to carry out system-level modelling has the potential to create a necessary ability to work with scenarios as part of the work towards reaching the countrys energy goals. • REP 2 Ethiopia: Accessing Industry Energy Source Type and Energy Consumption Data which focused on energy efficiency addressed the industrial sector. Unfortunately, this project was not completed, but has nevertheless contributed to making the need to develop energy management more visible. This includes the need for available data on indicators of energy use for various sectors, an important step in making energy-intensive activities more efficient and thus creating the conditions for a sustainable energy system. • REP 3 Ethiopia: Develop Appropriate Improved Cook Stove (ICS) for Two Emerging Regions (Benishangule-Gumuz and Somali Regions). This change project addressed addressed the problem of traditional cooking methods which require large amounts of wood and charcoal, contributing to deforestation and a dangerous indoor environment, among other things. By developing and testing an efficient stove for charcoal, the team demonstrated the improvement potential that exists and contributed to the development towards more energy-efficient cooking with appliances that are adapted to the local context and cooking customs in the two regions targeted in the Change Project. The results were handed over to the responsible authority where it was further integrated into the ongoing project Emerging Regions Household Cooking Energy Efficiency Improvement.
2. Kenya The programme involved in total 26 participants and Kenya was represented in all programme cohorts. Three participants did not complete the programme. The Country Teams from Kenya implemented four Change Projects addressing relevant problems in the energy sector. • REP 1 Kenya: Energy Storage for Enhancement of Uptake of Variable Renewable Energy Grid Connected and Stand-Alone Systems • REP 2 Kenya: Development of Guidelines for Efficient Utilization of Biomass • REP 3 Kenya: Establishment of a Framework for a Repository for Data and Information on Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency • REP 4 Kenya: Framework for Public-Private Collaboration on The Development of E-Mobility Charging Infrastructure in Kenya All projects were highly relevant to the development of renewable energy in the country. The teams from Kenya were very committed to the programme and the planning and implementation of the Change Projects worked very well. The mentors noted a great commitment and a strong will to contribute to the projects aiming at making real impact. The process of anchoring and engaging key stakeholders yielded concrete results. For example, the energy storage project resulted in the World Bank carrying out procurement of a study entitled Kenya Battery Energy Storage System Options Study. Another example is the Change Project Framework for Public-Private Collaboration on The Development of E-Mobility Charging Infrastructure in Kenya which contributed to the initiation of the process of the development of the Kenya Electrical Vehicle Policy. An assessment is that the relatively large number of committed participants, in combination with relevant and well-executed Change Projects, has contributed to the interventions goal of impact.
3. Mozambique The programme involved 10 participants from Mozambique, out of which one person dropped out. Mozambique was represented in the first two programme batches (REP 1 and REP 2). The Country Teams from Mozambique implemented two Change Projects that addressed different problems in the energy sector in the country. • REP 1 Mozambique: Update on Mozambican National Energy Grid Code to Cover Renewable Energy • REP 2 Mozambique: Development of Viable Financing Mechanisms and Suitable Business Models for Renewable Energy Projects in Mozambique. The first Change Project addressed the need to develop a regulatory framework to cover a guideline of minimum requirements for the grid code to integrate intermittent renewable energy generation plants, such as solar and wind, to the national grid. The Country Team of REP 1 reviewed existing relevant documents and carried out a benchmark study comparing the grid codes of South Africa, Tanzania, Kenya, as well as the revision on grid codes done by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA). Their findings were shared with key stakeholders and was an important input for the Ministry of Mineral Resources and Energy (MIREME) in their work with drafting Mozambiques first grid code on renewables. The Renewable Energy Network Code was approved in November 2023. The work carried out by the team was also an input to the Energy Regulation Authoritys (ARENE) work in drafting general regulations for off-grid systems, including conditions for future connection of off-grid systems to the national grid. The second project addressed the obstacles for the private sector to develop projects within renewable energy in Mozambique. The Government of Mozambique has recognised that the private sector has an important role to play when Mozambique is diversifying its energy mix and therefore invited private project developers to sell electricity to the state-owned national power utility EDM. The team developed a discussion document for a guideline on how to develop on-grid Renewable Energy Projects in Mozambique. The document functions as a guide for potential investors in renewable energy projects as it provides data and information on the energy sector and its key actors, the regulatory framework, as well as describes what steps an investor needs to go through to develop a renewable project in Mozambique. Both projects contributed to creating better conditions for renewable energy to be developed in Mozambique with an increased understanding of the challenges that exist and increased collaborations with key stakeholders to have the results taken forward after the end of the REP programme.
4. Rwanda The intervention involved 10 participants from Rwanda who participated in REP 3 and REP 4, out of which 9 completed the programme. The represented organisations corresponded well with the organisations identified as strategic for the development of renewable energy in the country. The Country Teams from Rwanda implemented two Change Projects that addressed different problems in the energy sector in the country. • REP 3 Rwanda: Reduction of High-end User Tariffs for Mini-grid Sub-Sector • REP 4 Rwanda: Framework for the Implementation of Street Lighting in Rwanda Both Country Teams from Rwanda developed relevant Change Projects, but the teams had some challenges in concretizing and implementing their Change Projects. Both teams, but especially REP 3, had difficulty in taking decisions and carrying the project forward. It is believed that this could be a reflection of the situation in the country, with a weak civil society, limited media freedom, and non-existent political opposition, producing citizens afraid of making mistakes and taking their own initiatives. It is also noted that the commitment to the programme from several of the participants was relatively low in comparison with participants from other countries. The assessment is that the programme contributed to increased knowledge on an individual level, but most likely not on an organisational level. These conclusions, together with the fact that only a small number of participants took part from Rwanda concludes that it is difficult to see how the programme could have any major impact on the development of renewable energy in the country.
5. Uganda The programme involved 12 participants from Uganda who participated in REP 3 and REP 4. The organisations represented correspond well with the organisations that during the second Inception Phase were identified as strategic for the development of renewable energy in the country. Both teams implemented projects focused on clean cooking. • REP 3 Uganda: Improving Awareness for Electricity Cooking for Adoption of Renewable Energy in Uganda • REP 4 Uganda: Framework for the Adaptation of Electric Pressure Cookers Through Enhanced Financing Initiatives Both Country Teams in Uganda focused their Change Projects on the challenge of the lack of access to clean cooking. The country experiences rapid deforestation as trees are cut down to be used as cooking fuel while there is an excess generation of electricity. The two completed projects addressed different parts of this problem. The first project focused on creating awareness about the possibilities with electric pressure cookers, while the second project looked at financing models that could contribute to increased use of electric pressure cookers. The projects were also well in line with the countrys strategies where, among other things, a special tariff has been introduced to promote cooking with electricity. Ugandas two projects are an interesting example of the participants seeing value in building on the insights from the previous groups project. An assessment is that the programme, despite the relatively few participants, may lead to long-term impact as the participating strategic organisations increased cooperation as a result of the completed projects. The second project has created interest in the financing institutes in Uganda to develop financial products for the clean cooking sector.
6. Zambia The programme involved 14 participants from Zambia who participated in REP 1, REP 2 and REP 4. The fact that several participants from the Rural Electrification Authority and Zambia Electricity Supply Corporation (ZESCO) participated in the programme creates conditions for achieving change at the organisational level. • REP 1 Zambia: Provision of Adequate Information for Investment in Renewable Energy • REP 2 Zambia: Enhancement of Energy Efficiency in Zambias Households • REP 4 Zambia: Consumer Sensitization of Quality Low-Cost Solar Photovoltaic Products in Rural Communities of Zambia. The participants in both REP 2 and REP 4 carried out ambitious work with their Change Projects. The Country Team in REP 2 created a benchmark of the household consumption of electricity using data from ZESCO. This demanded a tremendous amount of work, getting hold of data and then analysing this big amount of data. It is the first time this type of analysis has been done in Zambia and the work will give a good base for ZESCO to promote energy efficiency since they now know more about the different consumption patterns. REP 4 focused on the problem of sub-standard solar products being sold to rural residents. The team interviewed rural households, collecting data from four different provinces. These households often have a low level of education and a difficult financial situation, which makes them extra vulnerable to the increased presence of sub-standard products on the market. This is a very pressing issue that also applies to other products. Efforts that counteract the countries in Africa becoming a market for sub-standard products are essential in several different ways. In addition to not creating the value they should, these products contribute to increasing e-waste, and to eroding poor peoples finances. With the knowledge that the team acquired from desk reviews of existing standards and gaps, interviews with key stakeholders, and data analysis from interviews with rural households, they were able to provide a set of recommendations and actions to take on how to improve the quality of solar photo voltaic products in Zambia.
7. Zimbabwe The programme involved 14 participants from Zimbabwe who participated in REP 1, REP 2 and REP 3. All the participating organisations were assessed as strategic, but there was a wider range of organisations taking part in the programme in Zimbabwe compared to the other countries. One conclusion is that so many organisations were able to participate in the programme but it also entails a risk as a smaller number of participants in each organisation would make it more challenging to advocate and lead institutional change processes. • REP 1 Zimbabwe: Increased uptake of Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency in Zimbabwe • REP 2 Zimbabwe: Low Adoption of RE Products in Rural Areas (Focus on Local Government) • REP 3 Zimbabwe: Solar Powered Commercial Irrigation Scheme: Productive Use of RE. The team from REP 1 focused on governmental level by targeting laws on duty and VAT. The REP 1 team addressed the lack of access to affordable and clean energy by lobbying for zero duty and VAT on renewable energy and energy efficiency products since they had identified this as one of the obstacles to increase the uptake. One of the participants was involved in the proposal to harmonize tax codes and standardization of duties and exemptions in SADC. Today, years later, the VAT Study Report has been finalized, financed by the Zimbabwe Energy Regulatory Authority (ZERA), and presented to the Ministry of Energy and Power Development. The REP 2 Country Team identified the local government as an important player to increase renewable energy. The team developed a framework for capacity building programme for rural local authorities and enrolled influential stakeholders for the eventual roll out of the capacity building programme. The REP 3 team focused on private sector and productive use of renewable energy through local farmers. They managed to develop a bankable project for a solar powered commercial irrigation scheme including a step-by-step guide on how to design a solar irrigation scheme as well as a user-friendly financial model that interested farmers can easily adopt and customize. Throughout the project the team successfully engaged key stakeholders, including the Zimbabwe Electricity Transmission and Distribution company, who decided to blend their traditional electrification methods with off-grid solar systems to target productive clients.
Specific results achieved during 2023-2024 Results for this last year of the REP show for participated countries Kenya, Mozambique, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe with total 30 participants (17 men and 13 women). Ethiopia was left out due to the experience of several participants dropping out of the previous programmes, and the increased instability in the country at large. With a regional phase in Zambia during May 2023 and Sweden phase during October 2023 as well as a digital final workshop during February 2024, the participants got training and work with their change projects. The ITP training focused on understanding the dimensions of sustainable development, environmental and social impact assessment, situation analysis in the field of renewable energy and energy efficiency in each country, grid integration aspects of renewable energy, green hydrogen, energy markets and a changing energy landscape, climate financing, project management, risk management, communication.
The change projects worked by country team show the following results:
- Kenya: The Kenyan team focused their Change Project on the development of e-mobility charging infrastructure. The team identified a need to address the transport sector to make it possible for Kenya to reach the goal of achieving 100% clean energy by 2030. The Change Project was initiated to formulate a framework for public-private collaboration on the development of e-mobility charging infrastructure aiming at providing guidelines on: a) Development of Electric Vehicles charging infrastructure; b) Collaborative financing approach for the development of EV charging infrastructure; c) Collaborative approach for mapping charging locations. The results were that interactions between actors in the change project contributed to sustainable mobility in the transportation sector, with the private sector as the doers and funders, and the public sector as the enabler through ensuring that the right standards. The impacts made from this change project is that a collaborative Public-Private approach to EV-charging infrastructure development is created to trigger the much-needed investment in the EV space leading to a sustainable transportation sector in Kenya and as a result, promote faster achievement of the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).
- Rwanda: The team from Rwanda implemented a Change Project that aimed to improve the coordination in the development and implementation of streetlighting projects in Rwanda. The background to the project is that the Government of Rwanda plans to have 100% energy access by 2024. This includes ensuring that all districts, sectors, and homes are given access to modern electricity using grid and off-grid technology solutions. Energy access also includes public lighting for roads and streets, productive use facilities, community centres, and other strategic locations across the country. This project resulted in a guiding document for the planning, implementation, and maintenance of street lighting infrastructure across the country. The result is a set of recommendations and procedures that address various aspects of street lighting, contributing to uniformity, sustainability, and efficiency in the development of street lighting in Rwanda. The impact from this change project is to contribute to the development where a safer, more efficient, and sustainable urban environment is created.
- Tanzania: The Change Project team examined how solar photovoltaics (PV) could be used in commercial centres. The project aim was to increase the utilization of solar photovoltaic systems in commercial establishments by raising awareness about the benefits of renewable energy and educating businesses about Solar PV technology and its potential. The unreliable supply of electricity from the grid makes it necessary to use generators as a back-up system in commercial centres. This entails the use of fossil fuels, high operation costs, energy inefficiency, and high carbon emissions in urban setups. Therefore, A case study was carried out for integrating solar PV in Mlimani City Mall to investigate economic, environmental, and social aspects. The result from this change project demonstrated economic advantages through sustained cost savings and revenue generation opportunities by a shift from traditional energy sources to a cleaner, sustainable future.
- Uganda: The Change Project aimed at creating a structure that would encourage the extensive adoption of electric pressure cookers (EPCs) in Uganda, with a specific focus on addressing affordability challenges to increase accessibility to energy. The core objectives involved devising creative financing solutions, enhancing awareness to promote EPC adoption, cultivating partnerships, advocating for policy backing, and implementing continuous impact monitoring for improvement. The result of this change project is development of a comprehensive framework, extensive stakeholder engagement, policy integration, increased public awareness of EPCs and their benefits, financial institution participation and interest in providing financial products that support customers to purchase EPCs in an economically friendly way, government support, and the initiation of pilot programmes to test the effectiveness of the framework. This has contributed to noticeable cost savings experienced by consumers, increased use of energy efficiency practices and equipment while cooking, positive environmental impact. The impacts generated from the results show the need for adapted financing structures to enable a technology shift to clean cooking methods. The expected impacts of the project include the widespread adoption of EPC which would lead to increased use of energy efficient cooking appliances thereby reducing energy waste at the household level and contributing to overall grid efficiency and stability.
- Zambia: The Change Project in Consumer Sensitization of Quality Low-Cost Solar Photovoltaic Products in Rural Communities of Zambia contributed to address the problem of inadequate awareness of solar PV products on the market specifically for rural consumers. Increased awareness would result in rural consumers purchasing more high-quality solar PV product which would lead to more high-quality solar PV products on the market. The key results of the project comprised affordability, energy needs, and consumer awareness. The results also showed that the number of people living in a household influenced the households energy needs and hence the off-grid solar PV energy solution. The impacts of this change project is that educated rural communities about quality solar PV products would result in better choices when purchasing these products and this would result in rural communities that could challenge the agents and others and only settle for high quality solar PV products. This is expected to influence the quality of solar PV products on the market. The increase in quality solar Pico and Solar Home Systems would result in increased confidence in off-grid solar PV solutions and, therefore, more households would be attracted to solar renewable energy solutions.
